title: Convert Doubly Linked List to Array II
statement:
A doubly linked list stores integers. Each node has a value `val`, a pointer `next` to the node after it (`null` at the tail) and a pointer `prev` to the node before it (`null` at the head). You are handed `node`, which can be any node of the list, not necessarily the first one. Return an array holding every value of the list, ordered from the head to the tail. Leave the list's pointers unchanged.

Each case is written as `[node, head]`: the value of the given node (all values are distinct), then the values of the whole list from head to tail. Your function is called as `toArray(node)` with the node object only; `head` is not passed to it. (The TypeScript starter types the node as `_Node`, which does not list `prev`; the objects still have it.)
constraints: The list has between 1 and 500 nodes
node is a node of the list
notes:
## Intuition

Reading a linked list in order needs its head, but here we only hold some node, possibly in the middle. The `prev` pointers lead back to the head, and from there an ordinary forward walk along `next` meets every value in order. Another way, used by the brute force, is to read the values before `node` backwards, reverse them, and append the values from `node` onwards.

## Approach

1. Set `head` to `node` and follow `prev` while it is not `null`; the node without a predecessor is the head.
2. Walk `current` from `head` along `next` until it becomes `null`, pushing each `val` into `values`.
3. Return `values`.

## Example 1, step by step

The list is 1 ⇄ 2 ⇄ 3 ⇄ 4 ⇄ 5 and `node` holds 5, the tail. `head` steps back to 4, 3, 2 and 1, whose `prev` is `null`, so it stops there. The forward walk pushes 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, then `current` becomes `null` after the tail, and the answer is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): at most n - 1 steps back and n steps forward.
- Space: O(1) besides the returned array.

## Pitfalls

- Starting the forward walk at `node` loses every value before it.
- Loop on `head.prev !== null`, not `head !== null`, or `head` walks off the list and ends up `null`.
- Only read the pointers; changing `prev` or `next` breaks the list.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `head` | moves back from `node` until it is the first node |
| `values` | the answer, filled from head to tail |
| `current` | the node being read in the forward walk |
